scenes.purpose: Read the code section itself.

visual.description: The text of UCC 1-308(a) as a clean document page; the highlight sweeps across the reservation-of-rights clause as s19 is spoken.

citations.label: UCC 1-308, text and official comment

scenes.direction: Page slides in on s18; highlight on s19.
scenes.narration: Start with the code section, because you can read it yourself. UCC 1-308 says that a party who goes ahead and performs "with explicit reservation of rights" does not thereby give up the rights it reserved, and that phrases such as without prejudice or under protest are enough to do it.

scenes.purpose: Show what the official comment says the section is for.

visual.description: Same page, now at Comment 1; the highlight marks the machinery phrase.

excerpt.highlight: provides machinery for the continuation of performance along the lines contemplated by the contract despite a pending dispute

citations.label: UCC 1-308, text and official comment

scenes.narration: The official comment explains what that is for: it "provides machinery for the continuation of performance along the lines contemplated by the contract despite a pending dispute".

scenes.purpose: Make the section's ordinary use concrete, then show what it does not mention.

visual.description: Left half: a three-step strip drawn left to right, "Timber delivered" (a stack of planks), "Paid under protest" (an invoice with an amber UNDER PROTEST stamp), "Price argued later" (two speech marks). An arrow runs through all three and keeps moving, labelled "The contract keeps moving". Right half, on s22: three greyed words in a column, "Courts", "Criminal charges", "Consent to a judge", each with a small "not mentioned" tag that appears as it is spoken.

citations.label: UCC 1-308, text and official comment

scenes.direction: Strip builds through s21; right column through s22.
scenes.narration: Picture a builder who takes delivery of timber she thinks is the wrong grade: she can accept it and pay under protest, keep the job moving, and still argue about the price later. That is the whole job of the section: keeping a contract moving during a dispute. Nothing in its text or comment mentions courts, criminal charges, or consent to a judge's authority.

scenes.purpose: Show a federal appeals court answering the status argument.

visual.description: The Benabe opinion as a document page; the highlight lands on the jurisdiction sentence as s26 quotes it.

citations.label: United States v. Benabe, 7th Cir., 2011

scenes.direction: Page in on s25; highlight on the quote.
scenes.narration: In United States v. Benabe, the federal appeals court for the Seventh Circuit dealt with defendants who said their status put them beyond the court's power; the trial court dismissed those arguments. The appeals court's answer was blunt: whatever status a person claims, sovereign citizen, secured-party creditor or flesh-and-blood human being, "that person is not beyond the jurisdiction of the courts".

scenes.narration: It added that such theories "should be rejected summarily, however they are presented", and it listed its own earlier cases, one of which described a sovereign citizen defense as having "no conceivable validity in American law".

scenes.narration: And even if a fringe did mean something, the court said, it could not shrink the court's power, because jurisdiction "is a matter of law, statute, and constitution, not a child’s game". The Lux Law Firm, which explains these cases online, puts it simply: "There are no cases attributing any kind of legal significance to the fringes on a flag in an American courthouse".

scenes.purpose: Show the real 1871 act by its title.

visual.description: Quote card with the act's title, set like a statute heading.
onScreenText: "An act to provide a government for the District of Columbia"

citations.label: Metropolitan R. Co. v. District of Columbia, US Supreme Court, 1889

scenes.narration: Now the history lesson. In 1871 Congress did pass a law, titled "An act to provide a government for the District of Columbia", the federal district around the capital.

scenes.purpose: Show what the act made of the District, and who holds sovereignty over it.

visual.description: A three-tier hierarchy. Top box: "The United States" (sovereign power). Middle box: "Congress", labelled "supreme legislature". Bottom box: "District of Columbia", labelled "body corporate for municipal purposes", with three small tags beside it: "make contracts", "sue and be sued", "like any city". The bottom box and its tags build on s38; the top two boxes and the connecting arrows build down on s39, and a stamp "not changed" lands on the bottom box on "has not been changed".

citations.label: Metropolitan R. Co. v. District of Columbia, US Supreme Court, 1889

scenes.direction: Bottom box through s38, then top down through s39.
scenes.narration: In Metropolitan Railroad Company v. District of Columbia, the Supreme Court read it as making the District "a body corporate for municipal purposes", with power to make contracts and to sue and be sued, like any city. The Court held that the District's "character as a mere municipal corporation has not been changed", and that the sovereign power over it is lodged "in the government of the United States", with Congress as its supreme legislature.

scenes.purpose: Close the 1871 claim with the Court's own words on crimes.

citations.label: Metropolitan R. Co. v. District of Columbia, US Supreme Court, 1889

scenes.narration: It even spelled out what that means for anyone charged with an offence there: "Crimes committed in the District are not crimes against the District, but against the United States".
